questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Technology found outside the roadmap
questions.question: A risk practitioner at an insurance broker learns the marketing team has used an unapproved cloud survey tool for six months to collect client contact details. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess the tool's client data risk with its business owner
options.B: Have IT block the tool until the business owner reviews it
options.C: Approve the tool on the roadmap and assess it at year end
options.D: Report the marketing team's policy breach to compliance

questions.key_concept: Technology adopted outside the roadmap is assessed with its business owner against appetite before anyone blocks or approves it.
questions.pre_read: Notice how long the tool has been in use and what data it holds, then weigh the timing of each option.
questions.correct_explanation: An unapproved tool is a risk to understand before it is a problem to remove. Assessing the client data risk with the tool's business owner gives the risk an accountable decision-maker and shows, against appetite, whether the exposure needs urgent treatment. Blocking first acts before analysis: it may disrupt a working process, push staff to another workaround and still leave six months of collected data unassessed.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: blocking stops new exposure. But this is unapproved use, not a confirmed incident; acting before analysis can disrupt the business and leaves the data already collected unassessed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the tool clearly meets a business need. But approving now and assessing at year end leaves the client data risk unexamined for months.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the team broke policy, and the breach may need reporting later. Treating it as a conduct matter first leaves the client data risk unanalyzed and unowned.

tips: Eliminate: C approves the tool before any risk review, and D treats a data risk as a conduct issue before anyone knows its size.
Final two: A beats B because the practitioner analyzes the risk with its owner before acting; blocking first is a response chosen without knowing the risk.
Exam cue: for shadow IT found in use, the FIRST step is usually to assess the risk with the business owner, not to ban or approve the tool.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Legacy system risk
questions.question: At a county court service, the operations manager says a case-filing system on unsupported software needs no risk entry because it has not failed in twelve years. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Record the risk as low likelihood given its clean record
options.B: Log the risk in the register with an accountable owner
options.C: Have internal audit test the system before a register entry
options.D: Have the system owner order a scan before logging the risk

questions.key_concept: Legacy and unsupported systems belong in the risk register with a business owner, whatever their reliability record.
questions.pre_read: Separate the manager's evidence from the facts in the stem that drive the risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Unsupported software is a known exposure whatever its track record: no patches arrive, skills fade and the impact stays tied to court filings. Logging the risk in the register with an accountable owner makes it visible and gives someone the duty to decide on it; rating against appetite follows. A scan adds useful evidence for that rating, but waiting for it before logging leaves a known risk invisible and unowned.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the system has been reliable. But past uptime says nothing about missing patches; the likelihood of compromise rises once support ends, and the impact is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because audit testing is independent. But internal audit gives assurance and does not run the register; recording the risk is the risk function's job and should not wait.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: scan results sharpen the rating. But unsupported software is already a known risk, so it is logged and owned now, with the scan informing the analysis.

tips: Eliminate: A reads past reliability as low likelihood, and C waits on internal audit, which gives assurance but does not run the register.
Final two: B beats D because a known exposure is logged and owned first; a scan refines the rating but is not a gate before the risk becomes visible.
Exam cue: 'it still works' is never a risk assessment. Legacy and unsupported systems go in the register with a business owner, then get rated.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-02 (software is maintained, replaced and removed commensurate with risk)

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Change process findings
questions.question: After two outages, a risk practitioner reviews a retailer's change management process. Which of the following findings should concern the practitioner MOST?

options.A: Standard changes deployed without change board review
options.B: Low-risk normal changes approved by team leads
options.C: A change advisory board that meets once a week
options.D: Emergency changes that get no review afterward

questions.key_concept: Emergency changes are acceptable only when each one receives a timely after-the-fact review.
questions.pre_read: Sort the findings into design choices and real control gaps before judging which matters most.
questions.correct_explanation: Emergency changes may skip the normal approval path only because a review follows soon after. When none are reviewed afterward, untested or unauthorized changes sit in production unseen, a plausible cause of the outages. Standard changes without board review are working as designed: they are pre-approved, low-risk and run from a set procedure, so the missing check there is intended, not a gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it also sounds like missing review. But standard changes are pre-approved by design because they are low risk and follow a set procedure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because approval moves away from the board. But delegating authority for low-risk changes matches review effort to risk, which is sound design, not a gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because urgent changes cannot wait a week. But those go through the emergency route; a weekly board is normal practice, not a weakness in itself.

tips: Eliminate: C describes a normal board cadence, and B describes risk-based delegation of approval; both are design choices, not weaknesses.
Final two: D beats A because standard changes are pre-approved by design, while emergency changes depend on an after-the-fact review that is not happening.
Exam cue: when a control lets a step be skipped, look for the follow-up check that makes skipping safe; a missing follow-up is the real gap.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-128 Section 3.3.2 (Implement the Configuration Change Control Process: unscheduled changes are reviewed by the CCB as soon as practical); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Recurring service failures
questions.question: Check-in kiosks at a regional airline froze five times last month, and the service desk restored each within minutes. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: A tighter five-minute restore target for each kiosk
options.B: Replacement kiosks from a different vendor
options.C: A key risk indicator tracking kiosk outages
options.D: A problem record to identify the root cause

questions.key_concept: Incident management restores service; problem management removes the root cause of repeated incidents.
questions.pre_read: Notice how often the same failure returns and what each option would change about it.
questions.correct_explanation: Repeated incidents with the same symptom point to an unresolved cause. Incident management has done its job by restoring service; problem management now needs to find why the kiosks freeze so the cause can be removed through a controlled change, which lowers future likelihood. An indicator for outages is useful monitoring, but it only measures the risk; it does not reduce it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because faster restores shorten each disruption. But a tighter target improves incident handling and leaves the cause in place, so the freezes and passenger delays keep recurring.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because new hardware looks like a permanent fix. But replacing kiosks before the cause is known may not work; the fault could be software, network or configuration.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an indicator makes the trend visible to owners. But measuring recurrence does not stop it; the root cause still needs to be found.

tips: Eliminate: A speeds up incident handling without touching the cause, and B picks a fix before root cause analysis shows what is actually failing.
Final two: D beats C because problem management finds the cause so it can be removed, while an indicator only reports a risk that keeps recurring.
Exam cue: repeated incidents with the same symptom call for problem management and root cause analysis, not faster restores.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (problem); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an incident and the root cause of the incident); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-03 (improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures and activities)

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Acceptance testing roles
questions.question: To meet a launch date, a university's project manager plans to have developers run user acceptance testing on a new student-fees system. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Allow it if developers document each test case and result
options.B: Ask internal audit to review the test results before go-live
options.C: Have finance users run the acceptance tests before go-live
options.D: Delay launch until an external testing firm completes the tests

questions.key_concept: User acceptance testing is performed and signed off by business users, independent of the developers who built the system.
questions.pre_read: Ask what acceptance testing is meant to prove, and who is able to prove it.
questions.correct_explanation: User acceptance testing confirms that the system meets the business's needs, so the people who will rely on it, here finance users, should run it and sign off the results. That keeps the check independent of the builders and puts acceptance with the business. An external firm adds independence but cannot judge business fit, and delaying the launch is the sponsor's decision, not the practitioner's.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because records make developer testing reviewable. But developers still test against their own understanding, so the check is neither independent nor business-led.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because internal audit is independent. But audit gives assurance on the process, not acceptance of the system; reviewing results after the fact does not replace user testing.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: an external firm is independent of the developers. But only users can confirm business fit, and launch dates belong to the sponsor.

tips: Eliminate: A documents developer testing without making it independent, and B gives the job to internal audit, whose role is assurance, not system acceptance.
Final two: C beats D because acceptance is about business needs, so business users run the tests; outside testers are independent but cannot judge fit.
Exam cue: in SDLC items, developers build and test their code, business users accept the system, and owners accept residual risk.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Third-party AI model update
questions.question: A health insurer's chatbot vendor will replace the underlying AI model next month, saying the interface and prices stay the same. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Monitor member complaints for a rise after the swap
options.B: Accept the vendor's assurance that answers will not change
options.C: Validate the new model before members rely on it
options.D: Ask the vendor to keep the current model under contract

questions.key_concept: A vendor's change to the AI model behind a service is a change that needs validation before use.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the vendor says will stay the same, and what it does not mention.
questions.correct_explanation: A new model can answer the same questions differently even when the interface and price stay fixed, so the swap is a change to a member-facing process. Treating it as one means the new model is validated, for example with accuracy and harmful-answer tests, and the owner sees the results before members rely on it. Monitoring complaints is a useful second layer, but it detects harm only after members receive wrong answers.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: monitoring catches problems in production. But it is detective and late; members would already have received wrong or harmful answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor knows its own service. But behavior lives in the model, not the interface, and the insurer stays accountable for the answers its members receive.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it keeps a model the insurer knows. But vendors retire models as normal practice and may refuse; managing the change through validation is the risk-based step.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts the vendor's word that behavior will not change, and D tries to stop the vendor's change instead of assessing it.
Final two: C beats A because validating before use prevents harm to members, while complaint monitoring only detects it after the new model is live.
Exam cue: a new model, new training data or a retrained model is a change, even from a vendor; validate and approve it before go-live.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Approving a new data use
questions.question: A grocery chain's analytics team asks a risk practitioner about copying loyalty-card purchase records into a new reporting tool. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate approver for this new use?

options.A: The business manager accountable for the customer records
options.B: The risk analyst who assessed the reporting tool's security
options.C: The CISO, who sets the organization's data security policy
options.D: The IT manager who runs the database for the business

questions.key_concept: The data owner, an accountable business manager, approves access to and new uses of data; IT is the custodian.
questions.pre_read: For each person named, ask what their role lets them decide about the data.
questions.correct_explanation: The data owner, the business manager accountable for the customer records, sets the rules for using the data. They can judge whether the reporting use fits the purpose the data was collected for and its classification. The CISO sets security policy and advises on controls, but does not own business data or decide its uses; the IT manager is the custodian who carries out the owner's rules.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the analyst knows the tool's risks. But the analyst assesses and advises; approving a new use of business data is the data owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the CISO sets security policy and can advise on controls. But policy authority is not data ownership; the accountable business manager approves uses.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because IT runs the database. But IT is the custodian: it applies the owner's rules and cannot judge the data's business value or permitted uses.

tips: Eliminate: D names the custodian, who carries out the owner's rules, and B names the risk analyst, who advises but does not approve uses of business data.
Final two: A beats C because data ownership sits with the accountable business manager; the CISO sets security policy but does not decide business uses.
Exam cue: who decides access, use or retention of data? The data owner, a business role, not IT, security or the risk function.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Recordings kept past the schedule
questions.question: A bank's approved retention schedule says call recordings are deleted after three years, but the contact center holds every recording since 2017 because deletion was never set up. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask the data owner to extend retention to cover older recordings
options.B: Have IT set up the scheduled deletions, logging each run
options.C: Limit replay of recordings past three years to supervisors
options.D: Archive recordings past three years on lower-cost storage

questions.key_concept: Data kept past its approved retention period is exposure no one has accepted; the fix is disposal that actually runs and leaves evidence.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the data owner has already decided and why the recordings are still held.
questions.correct_explanation: The data owner has already set the period: three years. Every recording kept beyond it adds breach and legal-discovery exposure nobody accepted, and the cause is a deletion step never built. Having IT, as custodian, set up the scheduled deletions, excluding legal holds and logging each run, removes the excess and stops it returning. Limiting replay is the runner-up: it lowers misuse, but the recordings still exist to be breached or disclosed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because practice would then match the schedule. But it bends the owner's decision to fit a failed process; the period reflects business and legal needs, not what is stored.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since fewer people can replay old calls. But the recordings still exist, so a breach or discovery request still reaches them; the schedule says they should be gone.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because archiving cuts storage cost. But archived recordings are still held and still exposed; moving them changes the bill, not the risk.

tips: Eliminate: A rewrites the owner's schedule to fit a failed process, and D only moves data that should no longer exist.
Final two: B beats C because data past its retention period should not exist at all; limiting replay reduces misuse but leaves the exposure in place.
Exam cue: when data outlives its approved retention, the BEST answer makes disposal happen, with evidence, rather than guarding or moving the excess.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Investment prioritization
questions.question: A hospital's investment committee must choose between two projects with similar returns; one retires a system tied to a high-rated patient-safety risk. Which of the following inputs from the risk practitioner is MOST useful?

options.A: Each project manager's own project risk log
options.B: A ranking of the projects by return on investment
options.C: A new rating of the patient-safety risk against appetite
options.D: Each project's effect on the enterprise risk profile

questions.key_concept: Portfolio decisions weigh value and risk together, including the enterprise risk a project would reduce.
questions.pre_read: Note what the two projects share and what separates them, then ask which information shows that difference.
questions.correct_explanation: With returns roughly equal, the deciding difference is risk. Showing how each project would change the enterprise risk profile, including the patient-safety risk one would reduce, lets the committee weigh value and risk together and make the call. Re-rating the patient-safety risk, already rated high, sizes one effect but misses any risk the other project would reduce or add, so it cannot settle the comparison.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because project teams know their own risks. But project logs track delivery risks such as delay and overrun, not how each choice changes the enterprise's exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because return is the usual basis for investment. But it cannot separate two projects with similar returns, and it hides the risk reduction one of them offers.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it sizes the risk one project would retire. But the committee is comparing two projects, so it needs each one's effect on the whole risk profile.

tips: Eliminate: B ranks on return, which cannot separate projects with similar returns, and A offers project delivery logs that do not show enterprise exposure.
Final two: D beats C because the committee is choosing between two projects; rating one risk alone misses what else each project adds or removes.
Exam cue: in portfolio items, the practitioner gives decision-makers value and risk together, including risks a project would reduce; the committee decides.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Project risk log in Agile delivery
questions.question: A pension fund's scrum team has rated the risk of a weak access control that will remain after go-live and marked it accepted in its project risk log. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the scrum team to fix the access control next sprint
options.B: Record the team's acceptance in the register and monitor it
options.C: Take the acceptance decision to the accountable risk owner
options.D: Have the product owner hold the release until it is fixed

questions.key_concept: A delivery team cannot accept a risk it does not own; a weakness lasting past go-live goes to the accountable business risk owner to decide.
questions.pre_read: Notice who marked the entry accepted and how long the weakness will last.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk that will outlive the project becomes an operational risk, so a scrum team cannot accept it on the enterprise's behalf. Taking the decision to the accountable business risk owner, with the risk raised in the enterprise register, puts it with someone who can accept it within appetite or require treatment. Asking the team to fix it may be the eventual answer, but choosing the response first skips the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: fixing the weakness may be right. But the team would be choosing the response; the owner first decides whether to fix, compensate or accept.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recording keeps the risk visible. But logging the team's acceptance treats a delivery team as the risk owner; risk that reaches operations needs the accountable owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it keeps the weakness out of production. But a product owner runs the backlog, not operational risk; holding the release picks a response before the risk owner decides.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a delivery team accept an operational risk, and D has the product owner hold the release, a response chosen before the risk owner decides.
Final two: C beats A because the owner decides the response first; asking the team to fix it picks a treatment before the right person has weighed the risk.
Exam cue: when a project team marks a lasting risk as accepted, take the decision to the accountable risk owner; teams record risks, they do not accept them.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Shared recovery dependency
questions.question: A payroll provider's disaster recovery site is in another city but relies on the same internet carrier as its main data center. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess whether losing the shared carrier would breach the payroll RTO
options.B: Move the recovery site to a city served by a different carrier
options.C: Recommend that the owner fund a second carrier for the recovery site
options.D: Assess the carrier's outage history and service-level commitments

questions.key_concept: A dependency shared by primary and recovery sites is analyzed against recovery objectives before a treatment is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Look for anything the two sites have in common, then weigh what each option assumes is already known.
questions.correct_explanation: A shared carrier is a single point of failure that could take down both sites, but the size of the risk depends on what an outage would do to payroll. Assessing it against the recovery time objective (RTO) the business set for payroll shows whether the exposure is within tolerance and what treatment is justified. A second carrier may well be the answer, yet recommending it before analysis skips the cost-benefit judgment the owner needs.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a different carrier removes the shared dependency. But relocating is a costly treatment chosen before the risk is analyzed, and the RTO might be met far more cheaply.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: diverse carriers remove the shared dependency. But the practitioner first analyzes the impact so the owner can weigh the fix against its cost.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because carrier reliability bears on likelihood. But outage history and service levels describe the carrier, not what losing it would do to payroll.

tips: Eliminate: D gathers assurances about the carrier rather than the impact of losing it, and B jumps to a costly relocation before the risk is sized.
Final two: A beats C because analysis comes before treatment; the RTO comparison tells the owner whether a second carrier is worth its cost.
Exam cue: when a recovery design shares a dependency with production, first measure the impact against RTO and RPO, then recommend a treatment.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Ransomware restore sequence
questions.question: Ransomware has encrypted a distributor's order system, and the operations director urges an immediate restore from last night's backup to resume shipping. What should the risk practitioner advise FIRST?

options.A: Restore the order system from last night's backup
options.B: Contain the attack before the order system is restored
options.C: Pay the ransom if it costs less than the outage losses
options.D: Restore from an older backup made before the attack began

questions.key_concept: During ransomware recovery, contain the attack first, then verify the backup is clean before restoring.
questions.pre_read: Notice the pressure in the stem and what is still unknown about the attack.
questions.correct_explanation: Restoring while the attacker still has access, or from a backup that holds the malware, invites a second encryption and a longer outage. Containment comes first; the backup is then verified as clean, and only then is the system restored. An older backup lowers the chance of restoring malware, but without containment the attacker can simply encrypt the restored system again, and an older copy also loses more orders.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is fastest. But if the attacker is still inside or the backup carries the malware, the restored system is encrypted again.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it may look like the quickest way back. But paying is a senior management and legal decision, does not guarantee recovery and may breach sanctions rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: an older copy is less likely to hold malware. But without containment the attacker can re-encrypt it, and it loses more data.

tips: Eliminate: A restores into a live attack, and C reduces a legal and senior management decision about paying criminals to a cost comparison.
Final two: B beats D because containment must come first; an older backup restored without containment can be encrypted again and costs extra lost data.
Exam cue: in ransomware recovery the order is contain, verify the backup is clean, then restore; the practitioner advises on that order, and the incident lead and business owner decide.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Vendor claims for a new platform
questions.question: A retail bank's innovation team wants to adopt a blockchain trade-finance platform, citing the vendor's claim that it is tamper-proof. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Approve a limited pilot based on the tamper-proof design
options.B: Advise against the platform until the technology has matured
options.C: Assess the platform's risks and benefits for the bank
options.D: Assess the vendor's controls through independent certification

questions.key_concept: Emerging technology is assessed for both risks and benefits against objectives and appetite before adoption.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the vendor claims from what the bank still needs to know about its own use.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor's tamper-proof claim covers the ledger, not the bank's whole use: key management, smart-contract errors, legal standing and integration all carry risk, and the platform may also offer real gains. Assessing its risks and benefits for the bank, against objectives and appetite, gives senior management a basis to adopt, adapt or decline. Independent certification is useful evidence within that assessment, but it describes vendor controls, not fit.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a pilot limits exposure. But tamper evidence does not stop fraud through stolen keys or false data entered at the start, and approving is not the practitioner's call.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the technology's risks are still uncertain. But advising against it before any analysis forgoes possible value; uncertainty calls for assessment, not a reflex no.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: certification tests the vendor's claims. But it covers the vendor's controls at a point in time, not the bank's use, benefits or appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A takes the vendor's design claim as proof and has the practitioner approve, and B advises against the platform before weighing its risks or benefits.
Final two: C beats D because a fit-specific assessment of risks and benefits is the basis for the decision; certification is one input about vendor controls.
Exam cue: for emerging technology, assess both threats and opportunities against objectives and appetite before anyone adopts or bans it.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. High-impact AI before go-live
questions.question: A city council plans to rank housing-assistance applications with a vendor's AI tool that scored well in tests on the vendor's own data. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Accept the vendor's test results as evidence of the tool's fairness
options.B: Test the tool for bias and accuracy on past council applications
options.C: Have caseworkers review the rankings before decisions are issued
options.D: Limit the tool to applications from one district at first

questions.key_concept: High-impact AI is assessed on the organization's own data and use before controls are chosen or the tool goes live.
questions.pre_read: Notice whose data the vendor's tests used, and how serious the decisions are for the people ranked.
questions.correct_explanation: Housing-assistance rankings affect people's lives, and tests on the vendor's data say little about bias or accuracy for the council's applicants. Testing the tool on past council applications comes first, because it shows whether the risk is within appetite and which controls are needed. Caseworker review is a likely control, but adding it before the test chooses a treatment blind: reviewers would not yet know where the tool's rankings go wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor's tests were positive. But they used the vendor's data; the council stays accountable for decisions about its applicants and needs results on its own population.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: human review is a strong control for high-impact AI. But added before testing, it is a treatment chosen blind: reviewers cannot yet know where the tool errs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a smaller rollout limits harm. But applicants in that district would still face an unassessed tool; limiting scope does not replace assessment.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the vendor's own tests as proof for a different population, and D narrows the rollout but still runs an unassessed tool on real applicants.
Final two: B beats C because assessment comes before treatment; human oversight will likely be part of the answer, but only local bias and accuracy results show what kind and how much.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Conflicting duties
questions.question: A risk practitioner finds that one employee at a charity's finance office can add new suppliers, approve their invoices and release payments. Which of the following principles does this MOST directly violate?

options.A: Separation of duties
options.B: Least privilege
options.C: Defense in depth
options.D: Need-to-know

questions.key_concept: Separation of duties splits conflicting steps of a process so no one person can complete and conceal misuse alone.
questions.pre_read: List the steps one person controls, then match the risk to the principle each option names.
questions.correct_explanation: Adding suppliers, approving invoices and releasing payments are conflicting duties: together they let one person create a fake supplier, approve its invoice and pay it, with no one else involved. That is a separation of duties failure. Least privilege is the close runner-up, but each right might be justified for some finance role; the danger comes from combining them in one person.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the access is broad. But least privilege asks whether each right is needed; the real flaw is that one person holds every conflicting step.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because payments rest on one person's honesty, a single layer. But defense in depth is about layering different controls around an asset, not splitting duties in one process.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the employee can reach supplier data. But need-to-know limits what people can view; the risk here is completing a payment fraud alone, not viewing data.

tips: Eliminate: C concerns layers of controls and D concerns who may view information; neither addresses one person completing a whole transaction.
Final two: A beats B because the danger is the combination of conflicting duties; least privilege judges each right alone, separation of duties judges the set.
Exam cue: when one person can initiate, approve and execute the same transaction, the principle at stake is separation of duties.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Framework alignment and ratings
questions.question: A bank's latest framework assessment shows its cybersecurity practices meet the target profile, and the CIO proposes lowering every cyber risk rating in the register by one level. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Lower the ratings as the CIO proposes, citing the assessment
options.B: Lower the ratings for scenarios the improved practices address
options.C: Convert the profile's outcome scores into new risk ratings
options.D: Reassess each scenario on evidence before changing its rating

questions.key_concept: Framework alignment is evidence about controls; a risk rating changes only when the scenario's likelihood and impact are reassessed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a framework profile measures and what a risk rating measures.
questions.correct_explanation: A profile shows which framework outcomes the bank achieves; it does not measure the likelihood and impact of each risk scenario. A register rating records current risk, so it changes only when that scenario is reassessed on evidence such as control test results, threats and impacts. Lowering the ratings for scenarios the improved practices address is closer, but it still moves ratings on alignment, not on each scenario's reassessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the assessment is recent and favorable. But profiles describe outcomes achieved, not exposure; a bank can meet its target profile and still face scenarios rated high.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it targets the scenarios the practices touch. But it still lowers ratings on alignment alone; without evidence of the effect on likelihood or impact, no rating should move.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the scores are recent and structured. But they show which practices the bank achieves, not any scenario's likelihood or impact; converting them skips the reassessment they should inform.

tips: Eliminate: A treats framework alignment as proof of lower risk, and C turns outcome scores, which measure practices achieved, straight into ratings.
Final two: D beats B because a rating reflects a scenario's likelihood and impact; matching practices to scenarios is not evidence that either has changed.
Exam cue: framework alignment and certification are evidence about controls; a risk rating changes only when its scenario is reassessed.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Training matched to the role
questions.question: A parcel carrier gives all staff the same annual security course, yet four in five shared-login incidents involve seasonal warehouse workers in their first month. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Discipline seasonal workers found sharing a scanner login
options.B: Lengthen the annual course and run it twice a year
options.C: Add role-based login training to seasonal workers' onboarding
options.D: Lock warehouse scanners after one minute without activity

questions.key_concept: Awareness training is targeted at the roles and moments where the risk arises, not delivered as one course for everyone.
questions.pre_read: Notice which workers are involved in the incidents and when, then check when each option would reach them.
questions.correct_explanation: The incidents cluster in one role at one time: seasonal workers in their first month, who may start and leave before the annual course reaches them. Adding role-based login training to their onboarding puts the right content at the moment the risk arises. A longer or more frequent annual course adds volume for every role yet can still miss workers in their first weeks.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sharing logins breaks policy. But discipline treats a training gap as misconduct; new workers may never have been shown how scanner logins should work.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it adds training. But it adds volume for every role and can still miss workers in their first month, when four in five incidents happen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because an idle lock limits use of unattended scanners. But it applies to every worker and leaves the cause in place: new workers not yet trained on scanner logins.

tips: Eliminate: A punishes a training gap as misconduct, and D adds a general technical control that leaves the cause, untrained new workers, in place.
Final two: C beats B because the risk sits in one role at one moment; onboarding reaches new workers in their first days, while a twice-yearly course can arrive after their first month.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. New use of customer data
questions.question: A retailer collects purchase history for its loyalty program, encrypts it and restricts access, and marketing now wants to infer customers' health conditions from it for ads. What PRIMARY concern should the risk practitioner raise?

options.A: The encryption keys become a target for attackers
options.B: Marketing staff gain access to more customer records
options.C: Customer access requests extend to the inferred health data
options.D: The new use goes beyond the original collection purpose

questions.key_concept: Privacy governs whether a use of personal data fits its stated purpose; security only protects the data from unauthorized access.
questions.pre_read: Note what the retailer already does well, then ask what the new proposal changes.
questions.correct_explanation: Purpose limitation means personal data is collected for stated purposes and not used later in ways incompatible with them. Inferring health conditions from purchases for ads is a new and sensitive purpose customers never agreed to, whatever the encryption. Strong security keeps outsiders out but does not make an unfair use by authorized staff acceptable. Access requests are a real privacy right, but they follow from the use; they are not its main problem.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because keys guard the whole data set. But key theft is a security risk that existing controls address; the proposal raises how authorized staff will use the data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wider access raises exposure. But access can be limited to what the campaign needs; the deeper problem is whether this use is allowed at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: customers' right of access covers inferred data, a real privacy point. But it follows from the use; the problem is a sensitive new purpose customers never agreed to.

tips: Eliminate: A is a security concern about data that is already well protected, and B is about access scope; neither asks whether the new use is permitted.
Final two: D beats C because the proposal creates a new, sensitive use beyond the stated purpose; access requests follow from that use and are not its main problem.
Exam cue: privacy asks whether a use is fair and fits the stated purpose; strong encryption never answers that question.

options.D: Encrypt the workout data before it goes to the insurer

questions.key_concept: A privacy impact assessment is updated before new processing starts when purpose, data or recipients change.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the original assessment covered and what is new about the planned sharing.
questions.correct_explanation: A privacy impact assessment (PIA) describes the processing it assessed. Sharing workout data with an insurer is a new purpose and a new recipient, so the PIA must be updated before sharing starts, to judge the risk to members and show which protections the owner needs. Fresh consent may be one of those protections, but choosing it first skips the analysis that shows whether consent is the right basis or is enough.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because checking an assessment's scope is sound. But the change that matters is the processing, not the app version: a new purpose and recipient the launch assessment never covered.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: consent may be needed. But it is one possible measure; the updated assessment decides whether it is the right basis and what else is required.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the data is health-related and needs protection in transit. But encryption does not decide whether sharing it with an insurer is fair or lawful.

tips: Eliminate: A checks the app version when what changed is the processing, and D offers a security control that does not decide whether the sharing is acceptable.
Final two: B beats C because the assessment comes before the mitigation; consent may be part of the answer, but the updated PIA shows what is required.
Exam cue: a privacy impact assessment is updated whenever the purpose, data or recipients change, before the new processing starts.

questions.question: A law firm's partners want an AI contract-review tool that keeps client files in the vendor's cloud, against the target architecture; an architecture review board handles exceptions. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.B: Ask IT to block the service until the vendor changes design
options.C: Bring the deviation's risk to the architecture review board
options.D: Ask the review board to add the vendor's cloud after go-live

tips: Eliminate: A approves an exception on one control and outside the practitioner's role, and D asks the board to update the architecture only after go-live.
Final two: C beats B because a deviation from the target architecture goes to the review board with its risk; blocking first takes that decision before anyone weighs it.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Delayed retirement of a legacy system
questions.question: A port operator's register rating for an unsupported cargo database assumes it retires this year, but the project sponsor now reports an 18-month slip. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Re-rating the legacy risk for the longer exposure
options.B: Asking the sponsor to restore the original date
options.C: Keeping the rating while the replacement is funded
options.D: Logging the delay in the replacement project's log

questions.key_concept: Roadmap slippage that delays retiring weak technology extends the exposure, so the legacy risk is re-rated in the register for its owner.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the delay does to how long the unsupported system stays in use.
questions.correct_explanation: The slip keeps an unsupported database running 18 months longer, so a rating built on this year's retirement now understates the risk: likelihood grows as patches and skills fall away, and the exposure lasts longer. Re-rating gives the system's business owner a current basis to add compensating controls or accept the risk within appetite. wrong_explanations.B: Pressing for the old date may help; however, schedules are for the sponsor and steering committee to set, and the extra exposure needs rating whatever date is agreed.
wrong_explanations.C: Funding shows intent; however, a funded replacement removes no exposure until it is live, so the rating must reflect the unsupported database still in use.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the slip is useful; however, a project log tracks delivery risk, while the legacy database's exposure is an operational risk for the enterprise register.

tips: Eliminate: B tries to fix the schedule, which is the sponsor's decision, and C credits a funded plan as if the replacement were already live.
Final two: A beats D because the slip extends an operational exposure the enterprise register must show; a project log tracks delivery, not the legacy system's risk.
Exam cue: when a planned retirement slips, the legacy risk lasts longer; re-rate it in the register for the owner to act on instead of treating the delay as a project matter.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Unfunded permanent fix
questions.question: Problem management at a retailer traced repeated payroll run failures to an unsupported job scheduler; the $300,000 fix is unfunded, and staff rerun jobs by hand. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Close the problem record now that the workaround is documented
options.B: Ask the IT director to fund the fix from next year's budget
options.C: Have the scheduler owner add alerts for failed payroll runs
options.D: Present the payroll risk and fix options to the payroll owner

questions.key_concept: When a known error's permanent fix is unfunded, the risk and options go to the business process owner, who decides to fund, mitigate or accept.
questions.pre_read: Notice what problem management has already found and what decision is still open.
questions.correct_explanation: Problem management has found the root cause, so the open question is a business decision: fund the fix, add interim controls or accept the risk of manual reruns within appetite. That decision belongs to the payroll process owner, so the practitioner presents the risk and the options in business terms. Asking the IT director to fund it leaves a business risk with IT, which may defer it behind its own priorities.

wrong_explanations.A: A documented workaround keeps payroll running; however, the known error remains, and closing the record hides a recurring risk that no owner has decided on.
wrong_explanations.B: IT may be where the money comes from; however, whether the fix is worth $300,000 is a risk decision for the payroll owner, not an IT budget call.
wrong_explanations.C: Earlier alerts cut detection time; however, they treat the symptom and leave the root cause, the unsupported scheduler, in place.

tips: Eliminate: A closes the problem on a workaround while the root cause remains, and C speeds up detection of failures without removing their cause.
Final two: D beats B because the payroll owner bears the risk and decides whether the fix is worth funding; routing it to IT's budget skips that decision.
Exam cue: when a root cause is found but the fix is costly, take the risk and the options to the business owner of the affected process.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Rising emergency changes
questions.question: Emergency changes at an online retailer rose from 5% to 30% of all changes in six months; the on-call manager approves each, and each is reviewed afterward. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A second approver for each emergency change request
options.B: Analysis of why changes are routed as emergencies
options.C: More frequent change board meetings for normal changes
options.D: Monthly reporting of emergency change volume to IT leaders

questions.key_concept: A growing share of emergency changes signals the normal change path is being avoided; analyze why before adding approvals.
questions.pre_read: Notice which part of the emergency process works and what has changed.
questions.correct_explanation: A rise from 5% to 30% means the emergency route has become a normal path, and each case skips the full impact assessment and testing that normal changes get. The reviews afterward work, so the useful question is why teams use the route: slow approvals, poor planning or a way around scrutiny. Analyzing the cause lets the change manager fix it. More frequent board meetings guess at one cause.

wrong_explanations.A: A second approver tightens each emergency change; however, it adds weight to a path that should be rare and leaves the reason for the sixfold rise untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: Quicker approvals could help if delay is the cause; however, that is a guess until the reasons for the rise are analyzed.
wrong_explanations.D: Reporting keeps leaders informed of the trend; however, counting emergency changes does not explain why they rose or how to bring them down.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens approval on a path whose after-the-fact reviews already work, and D keeps counting the rise without explaining it.
Final two: B beats C because the cause of the rise is not yet known; more frequent board meetings fix one guessed cause.
Exam cue: when a control's exception path becomes routine, find out why before adding steps; the volume is a symptom, not the cause.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Servers missing from the inventory
questions.question: A logistics firm's endpoint detection console reports 1,240 servers, but its CMDB lists 1,020, and no team claims the other 220. Which of the following should concern the risk analyst MOST?

options.A: Detection licenses paid for servers the CMDB omits
options.B: Servers no owner patches, changes or backs up
options.C: Duplicate server entries in the detection console
options.D: Coverage reports that use the CMDB as their base

questions.key_concept: An asset missing from the inventory has no owner and sits outside patching, change and backup, so unknown assets are an operations risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice which source sees more servers and what it means that nobody claims them.
questions.correct_explanation: Operations processes such as patching, change control and backup work from the inventory. Servers the CMDB does not list, and that no team claims, are likely outside all of them, with no owner to fix or accept their risk. Duplicate console entries are the runner-up: they could explain part of the gap, but no team claiming the servers points to real, unmanaged machines, and reconciling them is how that is confirmed.

wrong_explanations.A: License cost is a budget issue; it says nothing about the exposure of servers no one manages.
wrong_explanations.C: Duplicates may explain part of the count; however, unclaimed servers are more likely real and unmanaged, and that exposure matters more than a counting error.
wrong_explanations.D: The reporting base matters for accuracy; however, the larger concern is the servers the base leaves out of every operations process.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about license cost, and D about how coverage is reported, not about the unmanaged servers.
Final two: B beats C because unclaimed servers point to real assets outside patching and change; a counting error is the less likely and less harmful reading.
Exam cue: an asset missing from the inventory is unowned and unmanaged; look for the exposure, not the bookkeeping.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Edits to an AI assistant's instructions
questions.question: A retailer's change policy covers code and AI model releases, but marketing edits the chatbot's instructions in production; one edit made it offer refunds the returns policy forbids. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Treat instruction edits as changes that need testing
options.B: Have the vendor filter refund offers out of chatbot replies
options.C: Limit instruction edits to the IT operations team
options.D: Review a weekly sample of chatbot conversations for errors

questions.key_concept: Edits to an AI system's instructions are production changes and need testing, approval and rollback like code or model updates.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the change policy covers and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: The change policy covers code and model releases but not instruction edits, yet the instructions shape what the chatbot tells customers just as code does. Treating each edit as a change means it is tested against the returns policy before customers see it and can be rolled back. A weekly review of conversations is the runner-up: it finds bad answers, but only after customers have received them.

wrong_explanations.B: A refund filter blocks this one error; however, the next untested edit could cause a different wrong answer the filter was never built to catch.
wrong_explanations.C: Restricting who edits narrows access; however, IT operations does not own the chatbot's content, and edits would still reach customers untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Sampling conversations is a useful detective control; however, it finds wrong answers only after customers receive them, while testing stops them first.

tips: Eliminate: B blocks only the refund error the last edit caused, and C moves edits to a team that does not own the content, still untested.
Final two: A beats D because testing an edit before release prevents wrong answers; sampling conversations finds them after customers are affected.
Exam cue: in an AI system, a change to prompts, instructions or settings is a change; it gets the same testing and approval as code.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Requirements for a purchased system
questions.question: A freight railway's project manager plans to set security requirements for a vendor maintenance system after the vendor is chosen. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A penetration test of the chosen system before go-live
options.B: The vendor's certificate as a security requirement
options.C: A risk assessment of the system once it is configured
options.D: Security requirements in the vendor selection criteria

questions.key_concept: For a purchased system, security requirements go into the selection criteria and contract before the vendor is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the plan sets requirements compared with when the key choices are made.
questions.correct_explanation: Requirements set before selection shape which vendors qualify and what the contract must promise; set afterward, they become change requests the vendor may refuse or price high, and gaps are accepted by default. Putting security requirements into the selection criteria lets each bid be judged against them. A penetration test before go-live still matters, but it can only find gaps in a system already chosen and paid for.

wrong_explanations.A: Testing before go-live is good practice; however, it finds gaps after the vendor is chosen and the contract signed, when fixing them is slow and costly.
wrong_explanations.B: A certificate is useful evidence; however, it shows a vendor met a standard within its scope, not that the system meets the railway's own requirements.
wrong_explanations.C: A risk assessment is needed; however, done after configuration it can only record gaps the selection has already locked in.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a vendor certificate as proof the system fits the railway's needs, and C assesses risk only after the choices are locked in.
Final two: D beats A because requirements set before selection prevent gaps; a test before go-live can only find them in a system already bought.
Exam cue: for a purchased system, security requirements belong in the selection criteria and contract; the earliest phase is the cheapest place for a control.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Scope change during design
questions.question: During design of a museum's ticketing app, the sponsor adds stored payment cards for one-tap repurchase, though the initiation risk assessment assumed the app held no card data. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Add card data controls to the build backlog for the next sprint
options.B: Ask the payment provider to confirm its card security certificate
options.C: Update the risk assessment for the stored card data
options.D: Pass the design gate and assess the risk before go-live

questions.key_concept: A scope change during the SDLC can void earlier assumptions; update the risk assessment before the next phase gate and before choosing controls.
questions.pre_read: Notice which assumption the earlier assessment rested on and whether it still holds.
questions.correct_explanation: The initiation assessment rested on the app holding no card data, and that assumption is now false, so its ratings and requirements no longer fit the design. Updating the assessment for stored cards shows the new exposure and the controls and compliance duties it brings, so the sponsor can decide whether the feature is worth them before the design is fixed. Adding controls to the backlog acts before anyone knows which controls the risk needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Card data controls will likely be needed; however, choosing them before the risk is assessed may miss duties the stored cards bring or add controls they do not need.
wrong_explanations.B: The provider's certificate covers its own checkout; however, the app will now store cards itself, so that evidence says nothing about the new exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Assessing later still happens; however, passing the gate on an outdated assessment fixes the design first, and gaps found near go-live cost more and are often accepted by default.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the provider's evidence for card data the app will now hold itself, and D lets the design be fixed before its new risk is assessed.
Final two: C beats A because the changed risk is assessed before controls are chosen; adding backlog items first guesses at what the stored cards need.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Retrained model with unknown training data
questions.question: Monitoring showed a water utility's leak-prediction model got worse after retraining, and the data team cannot tell which data set trained it. Which of the following gaps does this MOST directly reveal?

options.A: No record linking model versions to training data
options.B: No fixed schedule for retraining the model
options.C: Weak access control over the training data store
options.D: No human review of the model's leak predictions

questions.key_concept: AI training data needs lineage: each model version is linked to the exact data that trained it, so faults can be traced and versions compared.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the stem states as fact from what might have caused the problem.
questions.correct_explanation: The stem gives one hard fact: nobody can say which data set trained the live model. That is a missing lineage record, which links each model version to the exact data used, so the team cannot trace the fault, compare versions or roll back with confidence. Weak access control is the runner-up: tampering could explain a worse model, but the stem gives no sign of it, while the missing record is certain.

wrong_explanations.B: A retraining schedule controls when models are refreshed; however, the problem here is not timing but that nobody can trace which data produced the live version.
wrong_explanations.C: Tampering with training data can degrade a model; however, nothing in the stem points to it, and any investigation first needs to know which data was used.
wrong_explanations.D: Human review can catch bad predictions; however, it oversees outputs and would not tell the team which data produced the worse model.

tips: Eliminate: B concerns when retraining happens, not what it used, and D reviews outputs without showing which data trained the model.
Final two: A beats C because the stem states the lineage gap as fact; tampering is a possible cause the stem gives no sign of.
Exam cue: for MOST directly, pick the gap the stem's facts prove, not one that might explain the event; training data needs lineage to each model version.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Records no business unit claims
questions.question: During a data inventory, a university's risk analyst finds a shared drive holding 20,000 alumni records that no department claims. What is the analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Have IT classify the records and restrict access to them
options.B: Have IT delete the records under the default retention period
options.C: Name the IT director as owner of the alumni records
options.D: Ask senior management to assign an owner for the records

questions.key_concept: Every data set needs a business owner who decides classification, access and retention; unclaimed data is reported so senior management can assign one.
questions.pre_read: Notice who would normally decide about these records and whether that person exists.
questions.correct_explanation: Data belongs to the business, and its owner decides classification, access and retention. With no department claiming the alumni records, nobody can make those decisions, so the gap goes to senior management, who assign owners. IT may protect the drive meanwhile as custodian, but having IT classify the records is the runner-up: it makes the custodian decide what only an owner should, and leaves the ownership gap open.

wrong_explanations.A: Restricting access is sensible interim protection; however, classification is the owner's decision, and IT making it leaves the records with nobody accountable.
wrong_explanations.B: Unneeded data should not be kept; however, deleting records nobody has assessed may breach legal or business duties, and retention is the owner's call.
wrong_explanations.C: IT runs the drive; however, hosting makes IT the custodian, not the owner accountable for how alumni data is used and kept.

tips: Eliminate: B disposes of data before any owner has set its retention, and C confuses the custodian who hosts data with the owner accountable for it.
Final two: D beats A because only an owner should classify data; IT can protect the drive meanwhile, but it cannot fill the ownership gap.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Security work deferred in sprints
questions.question: A logistics firm's product owner has deferred security stories for six sprints so features ship first. Which of the following would MOST effectively prevent this in future sprints?

options.A: A risk team sign-off on security before each release
options.B: Security criteria in the team's definition of done
options.C: A dedicated security sprint before each major release
options.D: A quarterly internal audit review of the team's backlog

questions.key_concept: In Agile, security and control criteria in the definition of done keep risk work inside each item; the second line oversees rather than gates.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the stories could be deferred and which line of defense each option relies on.
questions.correct_explanation: Stories can be deferred because the team counts a feature as done without its security work. Adding security criteria to the definition of done makes that work part of finishing each item, so the first line builds the control into its own process. A risk team sign-off before release is the runner-up: it catches gaps late, and it has the second line running a gate it should oversee, not operate.

wrong_explanations.A: A release gate catches some gaps; however, it finds them at the end and puts the second-line risk team in the job of running a delivery control.
wrong_explanations.C: A security sprint keeps the work planned; however, it still pushes security to the end, where it competes with the release date again.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives independent assurance; however, a quarterly review finds deferrals months later and does not change how the team finishes its work.

tips: Eliminate: C still schedules security after the features, and D gives third-line assurance months later instead of preventing deferral.
Final two: B beats A because the first line builds security into its own definition of done; a risk team release sign-off makes the second line run the control.
Exam cue: in Agile, prevent deferred risk work by building it into the backlog and definition of done; the oversight lines check the process, not run it.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Open risks at project closure
questions.question: A ferry operator's online booking project is closing, and its project risk register holds three open security risks that will continue once the system is in operation. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Close the three risks in the project register at sign-off
options.B: Record the three risks in the lessons-learned report
options.C: Hand the risks to a business owner in the enterprise register
options.D: Ask the project owner to track the risks for another year

questions.key_concept: Project risks that continue into operation move to the enterprise risk register with an operational business owner when the project closes.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the risks end with the project or continue once the system runs.
questions.correct_explanation: Risks that outlast a project become operational risks, so they move into the enterprise register with an owner from the business that will run the booking system, where they are rated against appetite and monitored after the project team disbands. Having the project owner track them for another year is the runner-up: it keeps them visible for a while, but outside the enterprise register and only until the extra year ends.

wrong_explanations.A: Closing project risks is routine at closure; however, these risks continue in operation, and closing them leaves them with no owner or monitoring.
wrong_explanations.B: Lessons learned record what the project would do differently; however, they are not a risk record, so risks that continue in operation would have no owner or monitoring.
wrong_explanations.D: Extra tracking keeps the risks visible for a while; however, a project-side list sits outside the enterprise register, and the risks last beyond the extra year.

tips: Eliminate: A closes risks that continue in operation, and B files them as lessons learned, which no one owns or monitors.
Final two: C beats D because risks that continue in operation belong in the enterprise register with a business owner; a project-side list for a year sits outside the enterprise view.
Exam cue: at project closure, open risks that continue go to the enterprise register with a business owner; they do not close with the project.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. SaaS recovery gap
questions.question: A charity's SaaS donor database contract covers platform recovery but not restoring records that the charity's own users delete or corrupt. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Reliance on the provider's platform recovery for donor records
options.B: A charity-managed backup of donor records sized to the RPO
options.C: A contract clause moving data-loss accountability to the provider
options.D: Training for charity users on deleting donor records

questions.key_concept: Under shared responsibility, the customer stays accountable for its data and covers the recovery the cloud contract leaves to it.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly which recovery the contract covers and which it leaves to the charity.
questions.correct_explanation: Under the shared responsibility model the contract sets who does what, and here restoring records the charity's own users delete or corrupt is left to it. Accountability for donor data stays with the charity whatever the contract says, so the gap is closed with a backup the charity controls, set by the data loss it can tolerate. A contract clause is the runner-up: it might shift some cost, but it cannot move accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: The provider's recovery protects the platform; however, the contract excludes restoring records the charity's users delete or corrupt, so relying on it leaves that loss unrecoverable.
wrong_explanations.C: Contract terms can shift cost or work; however, the charity stays accountable for its donor data, and a clause does not restore lost records.
wrong_explanations.D: Training can cut accidental deletions; however, it cannot bring back records once lost, and corruption can happen without any user mistake.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on recovery the contract excludes, and D lowers the chance of user error without making lost records recoverable.
Final two: B beats C because accountability for data cannot be contracted away; the charity closes its side of the gap with a backup it controls.
Exam cue: in the cloud, read what the contract leaves to the customer; the customer stays accountable for its data and covers its side of the shared model.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Test scenario versus top risk
questions.question: A bank's IT operations manager plans the yearly failover test of its core system; the bank's top-rated risk scenario is ransomware that also encrypts online backups. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Advance notice of the test date to staff
options.B: A yearly cycle for testing the online backups
options.C: A test scope limited to the core banking system
options.D: No test assuming the online backups are lost

questions.key_concept: Recovery tests are tied to the register's top scenarios; a test that never exercises the highest-rated scenario leaves recovery from it unproven.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the test assumes with what the top-rated scenario assumes.
questions.correct_explanation: Tests should prove recovery under the scenarios that matter most. The top-rated scenario assumes ransomware has encrypted the online backups, yet no test assumes they are lost, so the bank does not know whether it can recover from the event it rates highest. A narrow scope is the runner-up: covering more systems helps, but testing them the same way would still leave that scenario unproven.

wrong_explanations.A: Unannounced tests add realism; however, planned windows are normal for failover tests, and advance notice does not leave the top-rated scenario untested.
wrong_explanations.B: Test frequency follows risk and change; however, testing the online backups more often would still never prove recovery once ransomware has encrypted them.
wrong_explanations.C: A wider scope would help; however, adding systems tested the same way would still leave the bank's top-rated scenario unproven.

tips: Eliminate: A and B concern notice and frequency, not what the test proves, so neither closes the gap against the top-rated scenario.
Final two: D beats C because no test assumes the online backups are lost, the condition behind the bank's highest risk; a wider scope without that condition proves no more.
Exam cue: judge a recovery test by the risk scenarios it exercises; the GREATEST concern is usually a top-rated scenario left untested.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Indicator for a backup control
questions.question: Which of the following should a risk practitioner propose as the BEST key control indicator for a magazine publisher's backup control?

options.A: Share of test restores that meet the RTO and RPO targets
options.B: Share of nightly backup jobs that finish without error
options.C: Number of ransomware incidents in the past year
options.D: Backup storage used as a share of capacity

questions.key_concept: A KCI shows whether a control achieves its purpose; for backups, that is test restores within RTO and RPO, not completed backup jobs.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the backup control exists to achieve before judging each measure.
questions.correct_explanation: A key control indicator shows whether a control is working well enough to keep risk in check. A backup control exists so data can be recovered within the business's recovery objectives, and only test restores measured against the RTO and RPO show that. Backup job success is the runner-up: it shows copies were written, but not that they can be restored, are complete or are fast enough.

wrong_explanations.B: Job success is worth tracking as a process measure; however, a job can finish cleanly and still produce copies that cannot be restored in time.
wrong_explanations.C: Incident counts show outcomes after the fact; however, they say little about whether backups work, and a quiet year proves nothing about recovery.
wrong_explanations.D: Storage use is an operational capacity measure; however, it shows nothing about whether the backups can actually be restored.

tips: Eliminate: C counts past incidents instead of measuring the control, and D tracks storage capacity, an operations measure.
Final two: A beats B because a backup control exists for recovery; restores tested against RTO and RPO show it works, while finished jobs only show copies exist.
Exam cue: a KCI measures whether a control achieves its purpose; pick the measure of the outcome the control exists for, not of its activity.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Pilot with little loss data
questions.question: A distributor's leaders approved a six-month pilot of augmented-reality headsets for warehouse picking, though little data exists on how they fail. What is MOST important for the risk practitioner to have agreed before it starts?

options.A: Loss data from other firms that use the headsets
options.B: Pilot controls matching those on live picking systems
options.C: Conditions under which the pilot would be paused
options.D: Vendor certification of the headsets' security

questions.key_concept: With little data on an emerging technology, run the pilot under pause conditions agreed from appetite with the business owner, limiting loss as evidence builds.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much is known about the headsets and what that means for planning their controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Little data means nobody yet knows how the headsets will fail in live picking, so controls cannot be sized with confidence. Agreeing in advance what would pause the pilot, such as error rates, injuries or data issues set from appetite with the warehouse owner, limits loss whatever happens while the pilot builds evidence to rate the risk. Copying the live systems' controls is the runner-up: it covers only failures someone has foreseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Other firms' losses add context; however, their sites and uses differ, and for a new technology that data is thin, so it cannot bound this pilot's risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Some controls will be needed; however, copying the live systems' controls assumes failure modes nobody yet knows and does not limit loss if the headsets fail in a new way.
wrong_explanations.D: Certification is useful evidence; however, it covers the product's security within a scope, not how the headsets fail in this warehouse's picking work.

tips: Eliminate: A borrows thin data from other sites, and D covers the product's security, not how the headsets fail in this warehouse.
Final two: C beats B because, with failure modes unknown, agreed pause conditions limit loss whatever happens; copied controls cover only failures someone has foreseen.
Exam cue: when an emerging technology has little data, pilot it under agreed limits and stop conditions set from appetite, and let the evidence firm up the rating.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Exit terms for a young vendor
questions.question: A logistics firm's evaluation of a start-up's drone delivery platform weighs benefits and threats; the platform would hold all route data in its own format. What is the GREATEST gap the risk practitioner should raise?

options.A: No exit terms if the vendor fails or is sold
options.B: No dollar value for each threat it lists
options.C: No check of the vendor's certifications
options.D: No pilot of the platform before the evaluation

questions.key_concept: Emerging technology from a young vendor needs exit terms, such as data return in a usable format; lock-in makes the vendor's failure the enterprise's outage.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the evaluation already covers and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: The evaluation weighs benefits and threats, but the deciding facts are a start-up vendor and route data held in its own format. If the vendor fails or is sold, the firm could lose the data and the service, so exit terms such as data return in a usable format and a transition period are the largest gap. Missing certifications are the runner-up: they matter for security, but they say nothing about surviving the vendor's failure.

wrong_explanations.B: Dollar values can sharpen the evaluation; however, a qualitative view is acceptable at this stage, and pricing threats does not address the lock-in.
wrong_explanations.C: Certifications describe the vendor's controls today; however, they do not protect the firm if the start-up fails or the data cannot leave its format.
wrong_explanations.D: Evaluating before a pilot is normal and helps set the pilot's conditions; it is not a gap in the evaluation.

tips: Eliminate: B prices threats without touching the lock-in, and D treats evaluating before a pilot as a flaw.
Final two: A beats C because the stem's risk is dependence on a young vendor's format; certifications show controls today, not a way out.
Exam cue: when a new technology locks data into one vendor, look for exit terms and data return before adoption.
